title: The Wedding
description: Shirley's first surviving comedy, a witty intrigue play in which the Duchess of Florence tests her suitors by pretending to favour the wrong man, and the various disguises and misunderstandings are resolved in a set of weddings.
plot_or_argument: The Duchess of Florence entertains several suitors, among them the noble Beaufort and the disguised soldier; through feigned favour, a fake death, and a discovered plot, the true lovers are matched and the court is reconciled.
narrative_structure: Five acts in the standard Caroline comedy structure of parallel love intrigues converging on a multiple wedding.
principal_characters: the Duchess of Florence; Beaufort; Rawliff; Gratiana; Jane; Annabel; Sir Ambrose Marlove
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with prose in the low comic scenes.
historical_context: First performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit c. 1626 and published in 1629.
literary_significance: Announces Shirley's characteristic mode — elegant, urbane intrigue comedy — and marks the transition from Jacobean to Caroline drama.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Shirley on the 1629 title page; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1629. Standard edition: The Complete Works of James Shirley (Alexander Dyce, ed., 1833); James Shirley, Plays (Cambridge edition, in progress).

title: The Changes
description: An early Shirley comedy of romantic change and constancy, in which lovers exchange and re-exchange partners before the final matching; it is Shirley's first play on the theme of inconstancy that would dominate his later work.
plot_or_argument: Two pairs of lovers in London and the country undergo reversals of fortune and affection, and the title's 'changes' resolve into a stable set of marriages.
narrative_structure: Five acts alternating between court and city settings.
principal_characters: Phillipa; Vincentio; Annibell; Clarinda; the Duke of Florence; Antonio
historical_context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit in 1626; published 1632.
literary_significance: One of Shirley's earliest plays and an example of the Caroline comedy of manners in formation.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1632. Standard edition: The Complete Works of James Shirley (Alexander Dyce, ed., 1833).

title: Hyde Park
description: Shirley's comedy of fashionable London society, set on the day of the horse races in Hyde Park, in which the wooing contests of the gentry, the tricks of a returned 'dead' husband, and the rivalry of suitors are resolved in a multiple marriage.
plot_or_argument: Three gentlemen compete for the hands of three ladies while a fourth, presumed dead, returns; the Park scene provides the public arena in which the rivalries are settled.
narrative_structure: Five acts, moving from the London lodgings to the Park and back.
principal_characters: Bonavent; Trier; Rider; Carol; Mistress Bonavent; Mistress Bonny; Juliet; Anne; the Hostess
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with prose in the comic low scenes.
historical_context: First performed at the Cockpit in 1632 and dedicated to Queen Henrietta Maria; Hyde Park had been opened to the public by Charles I in 1637.
literary_significance: A key document of Caroline court society and one of the earliest plays to make fashionable London topography its subject.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1637. Standard edition: The Complete Works of James Shirley (Alexander Dyce, ed., 1833).

title: The Lady of Pleasure
description: Shirley's most admired comedy, contrasting the extravagant, pleasure-seeking Lady Ariola Bornwell with the prudent and reformed Mistress Constance; it is the sharpest Caroline critique of conspicuous consumption and fashionable vice.
plot_or_argument: Sir Thomas Bornwell, disgusted by his wife's extravagance, pretends to leave her, while the virtuous Lord Lacywoth courts Constance; the Lady is finally shamed into reform and the couples are properly matched.
narrative_structure: Five acts with two parallel domestic plots of contrasted moral temperaments.
principal_characters: Lady Ariola Bornwell; Sir Thomas Bornwell; Constance; Lord Lacywoth; Celestina; Littleworth; Decoy
historical_context: Performed at the Cockpit in 1635, at the height of the fashionable London society that Shirley depicts and satirises.
literary_significance: Long regarded as Shirley's masterpiece and the finest comedy of manners before Etherege; its treatment of the extravagant lady anticipates Restoration social comedy.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1637. Standard edition: The Complete Works of James Shirley (Alexander Dyce, ed., 1833); also in Five Plays of James Shirley (Katharine M. Lea, ed., 1964).

title: The Antipodes
description: Shirley's fantastic dream comedy in which Peregrine, a man crazed by reading travel books, is carried to an imaginary antipodal world where everything is inverted, and is cured by the dream itself.
plot_or_argument: Peregrine, obsessed with Mandeville's travels, is drugged and conveyed to the Antipodes, a world of reversed customs and reversed theatre; the experience restores him, and the play ends with marriages.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a large embedded play-within-the-play occupying most of the second half.
principal_characters: Peregrine; Lord Letoy; Doctor Hughball; Diana; Martha; Joyce; the Antipodal king
literary_form: comedy; masque-comedy; play within a play
historical_context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at Salisbury Court in 1636 and dedicated to the Earl of Newcastle.
literary_significance: Shirley's most formally daring play and an important document of the Caroline fascination with travel, utopia, and the theatre's own conventions.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1638. Standard edition: The Complete Works of James Shirley (Alexander Dyce, ed., 1833).

title: The Traitor
description: Shirley's most successful tragedy, a political play on the assassination of the Duke of Florence by his favourite Sciarrha, loosely based on the murder of the Florentine Duke Alessandro de' Medici in 1537.
plot_or_argument: The Duke's favourite Sciarrha, ambitious and jealous, conspires with the Duke's rival to assassinate him; the conspiracy succeeds, but Sciarrha's sister Amidea refuses the Duke and the murder destroys both plotters.
narrative_structure: Five acts following the rise, execution, and ruin of the conspiracy.
principal_characters: the Duke of Florence; Sciarrha; Amidea; Cosmo; Lorenzo; Depazzi
historical_context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit in 1631 and read at court by Charles I, who is said to have remarked that it was 'a tragedy'.
literary_significance: The finest Caroline political tragedy and a principal influence on later plays of tyrannicide, including the Restoration heroic drama.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1635. Standard edition: The Complete Works of James Shirley (Alexander Dyce, ed., 1833).

title: The Cardinal
description: Shirley's last tragedy, written in Ireland and performed at the Cockpit in 1641, in which a scheming cardinal forces a marriage that leads to poisoning, madness, and death.
plot_or_argument: The Cardinal, thwarted in his own designs on the Duchess of Pavia, compels her to marry his protégé Columbo; when she loves the soldier Alvarez instead, Columbo kills him, and the Duchess poisons the Cardinal and herself.
narrative_structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a catastrophic denouement.
principal_characters: the Cardinal; the Duchess of Pavia; Columbo; Alvarez; Celinde; Hernando
historical_context: Composed during Shirley's Irish period and revived at the Cockpit in 1641, on the eve of the civil wars; printed in Shirley's Six New Plays of 1653.
literary_significance: A late and vigorous Caroline revenge tragedy, notable for its portrait of ecclesiastical ambition and for closing Shirley's career.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Six New Plays (1653). Standard edition: The Complete Works of James Shirley (Alexander Dyce, ed., 1833).

title: 'Tis Pity She's a Whore
description: John Ford's notorious tragedy of incestuous love between the siblings Giovanni and Annabella in Parma, and of Giovanni's murder of his sister and his entrance bearing her heart on his dagger.
plot_or_argument: Governing himself by passion rather than religion, Giovanni declares his love to his sister Annabella; she yields, marries the noble Soranzo to conceal her pregnancy, is discovered, and is killed by Giovanni, who then dies fighting Soranzo's followers.
narrative_structure: Five acts of a single, tightly driven tragic action with subordinate comic plots, ending in the public catastrophe at the cardinal's feast.
principal_characters: Giovanni; Annabella; Soranzo; the Friar Bonaventura; Vasques; Grimaldi; Bergetto; Philotis; Richardetto; Hippolita
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of sustained lyric intensity, with Ford's characteristic repetition and lament.
historical_context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Phoenix in Drury Lane, probably c. 1629-33, and published in 1633 with a remarkable author's dedication defending the play's seriousness.
literary_significance: The most powerful and most discussed Caroline tragedy; it pushed the theatre's moral limits further than any contemporary play and remains a central text in the study of early modern incest and tragic passion.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1633. Standard editions: 'Tis Pity She's a Whore (Simonetta de Filippis, ed., in The Works of John Ford, Manchester University Press); New Mermaids edition (Katharine Gillespie, ed.).

title: The Broken Heart
description: Ford's stately tragedy set in Sparta, in which the enforced marriage of Penthea to the aged Bassanes destroys her love for Orgilus, and the play ends in a chain of ritual deaths.
plot_or_argument: Orgilus, cheated of his love Penthea by her brother Ithocles' ambition, returns in disguise; Ithocles loves the Spartan princess Calantha, whose father the king dies; Orgilus kills Ithocles, Penthea starves herself, and Calantha dies of a broken heart.
narrative_structure: Five acts of a slow, ceremonially patterned tragedy in which the final scene of deaths is framed by the wedding masque.
principal_characters: Orgilus; Penthea; Ithocles; Calantha; Bassanes; the King of Sparta; Tecnicus; Christalla
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with lyric interludes and songs, of unusually measured and elegiac cadence.
historical_context: Published in 1633; probably written for a private playhouse or for court reading, given its restrained action and heavy lyricism.
literary_significance: Ford's most artistically controlled tragedy and the clearest Caroline example of a tragedy of honour, obligation, and emotional starvation.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1633. Standard edition: The Works of John Ford (Alexander Dyce, ed.); The Broken Heart (M. Joan Sargeaunt, ed.).

title: Love's Sacrifice
description: Ford's tragedy of unwarranted jealousy, in which the Duke of Pavy, persuaded by his secretary Nibrassa, believes his duchess Bianca unfaithful to him with his friend Fernando, and kills her before learning the truth.
plot_or_argument: The Duke marries Bianca but loves his friend Fernando more; Fernando and Bianca love each other chastely; the malicious secretary sows suspicion; the Duke murders Bianca and Fernando, then kills himself in remorse.
narrative_structure: Five acts following the Othello pattern of jealousy induced by a villain and resolved in catastrophe.
principal_characters: the Duke of Pavy; Bianca; Fernando; Nibrassa; Fiormonda; Colona; Petruchio
historical_context: Published 1633, performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Phoenix.
literary_significance: A notable Caroline reworking of the Othello situation, and an important example of Ford's preoccupation with honour and the destruction of innocence.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1633. Standard edition: The Works of John Ford (Alexander Dyce, ed., 1848); The Works of John Ford (Manchester University Press, 2012- ).

title: Perkin Warbeck
alternative_titles: The Chronicle History of Perkin Warbeck
description: Ford's 'strange truth' chronicle play on the Yorkist pretender Perkin Warbeck, who claimed to be Richard Duke of York and was received by James IV of Scotland before his capture and execution by Henry VII.
plot_or_argument: Warbeck, protected in Flanders and married in Scotland, asserts his claim to the English crown; Henry VII's cautious statecraft and the defection of Warbeck's supporters lead to his capture and execution at Tyburn.
narrative_structure: A five-act chronicle history with a double plot of state politics and Warbeck's personal constancy to his wife Katherine.
principal_characters: Perkin Warbeck; Henry VII; James IV of Scotland; Katherine Gordon; the Earl of Huntley; Lord Bacon; Sir William Stanley; Frion
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of grave, stateliest register.
historical_context: Performed at the Phoenix in 1634 and published the same year, dedicated to William Cavendish, Earl of Newcastle.
literary_significance: Ford's only history play and one of the last serious English chronicle dramas; it was praised by Weber and revived in the nineteenth century for its political seriousness.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Ford on the 1634 title page; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1634. Standard edition: Perkin Warbeck (Peter Ure, ed., Oxford University Press, 1939); The Works of John Ford (Manchester University Press).

title: The Lady's Trial
description: Ford's last surviving play, a tragicomedy in which Aurelio tests his wife Spinella's chastity, is deceived by the malicious Amoretto, and the trial is resolved by the intervention of Spinella's sister Castanna and the reformed Benatzi.
plot_or_argument: Aurelio's test of Spinella, engineered by the villain Amoretto, appears to confirm her unfaithfulness; the truth emerges when Castanna's own constancy is proved and Amoretto's imposture is exposed.
narrative_structure: Five acts of intrigue with a tragicomic resolution.
principal_characters: Aurelio; Spinella; Castanna; Amoretto; Benatzi; Fulgoso; Adurni
historical_context: Performed at the Cockpit in 1636 and published in 1639.
literary_significance: Ford's final play and a mature example of Caroline tragicomedy; its concern with the testing of female chastity connects it to the tradition from Boccaccio to Shakespeare's Cymbeline.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Ford on the 1639 title page; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1639. Standard edition: The Works of John Ford (Manchester University Press).

title: The Northern Lass
description: Richard Brome's first comedy, and his most popular, in which a young woman from the north of England, Bess Bridewell, is carried to London, falls among thieves and gulls, and is finally matched with her true love.
plot_or_argument: Bess, wronged and dismissed, travels south; mistaken identities, a robbery, and a series of comic adventures in London lead to her reunion with the noble Conrade and the punishment of the false suitors.
narrative_structure: Five acts of picaresque comic intrigue with songs and dialect humour.
principal_characters: Bess Bridewell; Conrade; Squelch; Anvil; Trainwell; Lackbeard; the Hostess
meter_and_prosody: Prose dominant with verse passages and songs; Bess speaks a Yorkshire dialect.
historical_context: Performed at the Blackfriars and the Globe in 1629; Brome was Jonson's servant and amanuensis, and Ben Jonson wrote commendatory verses for the 1632 quarto.
literary_significance: The play that established Brome's reputation and one of the most frequently reprinted comedies of the Caroline period; its regional dialect comedy is an early landmark.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1632. Standard edition: The Works of Richard Brome (Jane H. Steggle, ed.); Richard Brome Online Edition (Sheffield Academic Press).

title: A Jovial Crew
alternative_titles: A Jovial Crew; or, The Merry Beggars
description: Brome's most admired comedy, in which three gentlewomen run away to join a band of strolling beggars, and their idyll of freedom is tested by hunger, lust, and the law before they return home.
plot_or_argument: Rachel, Amy, and the widow Springlove's daughters abandon their comfortable homes for the beggars' life; the beggar community is ruled by the mysterious Patrico, and the experiment ends with marriage and the reintegration of the runaways.
narrative_structure: Five acts, alternating between the gentleman's houses and the beggars' barn, with an unusually detailed portrait of vagrant society.
principal_characters: Rachel; Amy; Meriel; Oldrents; Hilliard; Springlove; Patrico; Randall; Vincent; Martin
meter_and_prosody: Prose dominant, with songs and verses.
historical_context: Performed at Drury Lane in 1641, just before the theatres closed; the play was popular again after the Restoration and inspired several adaptations, including the ballad opera The Jovial Crew (1731).
literary_significance: Brome's masterpiece and the most substantial dramatic treatment of English beggar life in the period; it is a key text for Caroline social history and for the development of comic realism.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1652. Standard edition: Richard Brome, A Jovial Crew (T. H. Howard-Hill, ed., in The Works of Richard Brome).

title: The Sparagus Garden
description: Brome's comedy of London society set in the fashionable asparagus gardens of Lambeth Marsh, in which two country women come to London to better themselves and are drawn into the intrigues of the city and the garden.
plot_or_argument: Martha and Rebecca travel to London; Martha is seduced into a false marriage by the gallant Touchwood, Rebecca is courted by the honest Striker; the Sparagus Garden provides the social arena where the deceptions are exposed.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a strong topographical unity around the garden.
principal_characters: Martha; Rebecca; Touchwood; Striker; Annabel; Samuel; Lady Annabel; Snoop; the Host
historical_context: Performed at the Salisbury Court Theatre in 1635 and published in 1640; the Lambeth Marsh asparagus gardens were a notorious resort of fashionable London.
literary_significance: One of the sharpest Caroline comedies of urban topography and social mobility, and Brome's fullest treatment of the theme of the country woman in the city.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1640. Standard edition: The Works of Richard Brome (Sheffield Academic Press).

title: The Covent Garden Weeded
description: Brome's moralising comedy set in the newly built Covent Garden piazza, in which a reformed rake and his companions set out to 'weed' the district of its whores, pimps, and gallants.
plot_or_argument: Arthur Manly, the honest soldier, and his friends undertake to clear the Garden of vice; the plot turns on the rescue of the virtuous Rebecca from the brothel and the exposure of the pimps and gallants.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a strong reform plot and a satiric survey of the Garden's inhabitants.
principal_characters: Arthur Manly; Sir Nathaniel; Captain Ironside; Rebecca; Tria; Lady Blanche; the Pimp
historical_context: Performed at the Salisbury Court in 1632, in the newly developed Covent Garden district designed by Inigo Jones; published in the 1640 collection of Brome's plays.
literary_significance: An important document of the social history of Covent Garden and a notable Caroline attempt to moralise the city comedy of Jonson and Middleton.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1640 in Five New Plays. Standard edition: The Works of Richard Brome (Sheffield Academic Press).

title: Love and Honour
description: Davenant's tragi-comedy of love tested by honour, in which a noble lady disguises herself as a poor servant to try the constancy of her lover before the war separates them.
plot_or_argument: Evadne, beloved of the noble Prothall, disguises herself to test his faith; a series of misunderstandings, a supposed death, and a battlefield reunion resolve the conflict between love and honour.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a disguise-testing plot and a final recognition.
principal_characters: Evadne; Prothall; Alphonso; Melora; the Duke; Aurelio
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in 1634 and published in Davenant's collected Plays of 1639.
literary_significance: Davenant's first major success and a key example of Caroline tragicomedy; it also shows the beginnings of his interest in music and spectacle that would produce The Siege of Rhodes.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Plays of Sir William Davenant (1639). Standard edition: The Dramatic Works of Sir William D'Avenant (James Maidment and W. H. Logan, eds., 1872-4).

title: The Platonic Lovers
description: Davenant's comedy of fashionable Neoplatonic love, in which the court of the Duke of Florence practises a chaste 'platonic' devotion until nature and desire assert themselves and the lovers marry.
plot_or_argument: The courtly lovers vow platonic constancy; a series of tests, a mad scientist, and a soldier's blunt wooing expose the impossibility of the vow, and the play ends in conventional marriage.
narrative_structure: Five acts with parallel court and country plots.
principal_characters: the Duke of Florence; Eurithea; Philander; Cleander; Amadine; Theander; the Astronomer; Lycomedes
historical_context: Performed at the Blackfriars in 1635 and dedicated to Queen Henrietta Maria, whose court cultivated the Neoplatonic ideal of chaste love.
literary_significance: The principal dramatic treatment of Caroline Platonism and an important source for the intellectual history of the court of Charles I.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1636. Standard edition: The Dramatic Works of Sir William D'Avenant (1872-4).

title: Salmacida Spolia
description: The last masque performed at the court of Charles I, presented at Whitehall on 21 January 1640 with designs by Inigo Jones and with the young Prince Charles and his brothers among the masquers.
plot_or_argument: Discord, in the person of a malicious spirit, has troubled the land; Wisdom and the genius of Britain, embodied in the king, restore concord, and the masquers descend to dance with the ladies.
narrative_structure: The standard court masque form: antimasque of discord, main masque of harmony, and the revels.
principal_characters: Discord; Wisdom; the Genius of Britain; the masquers
meter_and_prosody: Verse and song with prose description; Inigo Jones's scenery and machinery.
historical_context: Presented at Whitehall in January 1640, months before the calling of the Short Parliament and the collapse of Charles's personal rule; Davenant had been made Poet Laureate in 1638 on Jonson's death.
literary_significance: The final Caroline masque and a poignant document of a court culture on the eve of destruction; it also marks Davenant's official succession to Jonson as laureate.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Davenant as laureate; Jones's designs are documented.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1640. Standard edition: The Dramatic Works of Sir William D'Avenant (1872-4); also in Orgel and Strong, Inigo Jones: The Theatre of Stuart Court (1973).

title: The Siege of Rhodes
alternative_titles: The Siege of Rhodes, Made a Representation by the Art of Prospective in Scenes
description: Davenant's 'representation by the art of prospective in scenes, and the story sung in recitative music', staged at his house in Rutland during the Commonwealth; it is generally regarded as the first English opera.
plot_or_argument: The Ottoman siege of Rhodes in 1522 is the historical frame; the love story of Alphonso, Ianthe, and Roxolana unfolds across five 'entries' (acts) of sung recitative and spectacular scenery.
narrative_structure: Five entries performed in painted perspective scenes with continuous recitative singing, no spoken dialogue, and a single female performer (Mrs Coleman).
principal_characters: Solyman; Alphonso; Ianthe; Roxolana; Mustapha; the Admiral
meter_and_prosody: Recitative verse in pentameter couplets and quatrains; the first sustained use of sung drama in English.
historical_context: Performed privately at Rutland House in May 1656 and publicly at the Cockpit in 1659, during the Commonwealth ban on public theatres; Davenant's innovations were tolerated because the work was billed as a musical entertainment.
literary_significance: The first English opera, the first English stage to use painted perspective scenery, the first to employ a professional actress, and the prototype of the Restoration heroic drama.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Davenant; the music was by Matthew Locke, Henry Cooke, Charles Coleman, and George Hudson.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1656; the Second Part in 1663. Standard edition: The Dramatic Works of Sir William D'Avenant (1872-4).

title: The Playhouse to Be Let
description: Davenant's Restoration burlesque comedy in five acts, each a parody of a different dramatic mode — French farce, English history, Spanish intrigue, opera, and the heroic play — with the notable introduction of the first professional actresses on the English public stage.
plot_or_argument: A playhouse is offered to let; each act presents a different burlesque entertainment, including a mock-Cromwellian history, a French farce, a parody of The Siege of Rhodes as 'The Cruelty of the Spaniards in Peru', and a send-up of heroic drama.
narrative_structure: Five self-contained acts framed by the playhouse-letting plot.
principal_characters: Sir Positive At-All; Caution; Sneaky; the Playhouse Keeper; the actors
literary_form: burlesque comedy; play within a play
meter_and_prosody: Mixed prose and verse, with songs.
historical_context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in August 1663 by Davenant's company; it records the moment when women first acted on the English public stage.
literary_significance: A valuable theatrical document of the Restoration transition and one of the earliest English stage burlesques.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1673. Standard edition: The Dramatic Works of Sir William D'Avenant (1872-4).

title: The Roman Actor
description: Massinger's tragedy of the Emperor Domitian, his love for the virtuous Domitia, and the murder of the actor Paris, framed by an elaborate defence of the theatre's moral function.
plot_or_argument: The actors are tried before the Senate on the charge of slandering the state; Paris defends the stage; Domitian, inflamed by desire for Domitia and by jealousy, kills Paris; the tyrant is finally assassinated by the Senate's agents.
narrative_structure: Five acts with three inset plays performed by the Roman company, and a courtroom defence of drama at the centre.
principal_characters: Domitian; Domitia; Paris; Lamia; Aretinus; Philargus; the Senators
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with prose in the inset plays.
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in 1626 and published in 1629; the play's defence of the theatre responds to puritan attack.
literary_significance: The most important early modern dramatic treatise on the function of the stage, embedded in a tragedy; it was revived by the King's Company after 1660 and was long Massinger's most admired play.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Massinger on the 1629 title page; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1629. Standard edition: The Plays and Poems of Philip Massinger (Philip Edwards and Colin Gibson, eds., Oxford University Press, 1976).

title: The City Madam
description: Massinger's comedy of a citizen's wife, Lady Frugal, whose ambition to be a lady leads her husband to fake a departure for the Indies and to test her virtue and her daughters' constancy.
plot_or_argument: Sir John Frugal pretends to embark for Virginia; Lady Frugal and her daughters, believing themselves rich, cast off their modest lives; the test exposes their vanity and they are sent to the colonies as punishment.
narrative_structure: Five acts of a Jonsonian testing-comedy with a moralising conclusion.
principal_characters: Sir John Frugal; Lady Frugal; Anne; Mary; Lord Lacy; Sir Maurice Lacy; Ramble; Luke Frugal
historical_context: Performed at the Blackfriars in 1632 and published posthumously in 1658.
literary_significance: Massinger's fullest treatment of London citizen society and one of the most striking Caroline comedies of female ambition and colonial punishment.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1658. Standard edition: The Plays and Poems of Philip Massinger (Oxford University Press, 1976).

title: Believe as You List
description: Massinger's political tragedy on the false Sebastian of Portugal, suppressed by the Master of the Revels for its treatment of a recent alliance and then rewritten; it survives in the author's manuscript with Sir Henry Herbert's annotations.
plot_or_argument: A young man claiming to be the lost King Sebastian of Portugal is recognised by many, pursued by Spain, and finally exposed as an impostor; the play explores the politics of belief and dynastic legitimacy.
narrative_structure: Five acts following the pretender's rise, recognition, and exposure.
principal_characters: Antiochus (the false Sebastian); Titus Flaminius; the Roman Senate; Marcella; Sulpitius
historical_context: First drafted in 1631 and banned by Herbert as seditious because of its allusion to the Anglo-Spanish alliance; Massinger recast the story in a Roman setting and the revised version was licensed on 6 May 1631.
literary_significance: The most important surviving manuscript of a Caroline play, documenting the workings of censorship; it is also Massinger's most serious political tragedy.
attribution_notes: The authorial manuscript is signed 'P.M.' and is universally accepted as Massinger's holograph.
bibliographical_notes: Authorial manuscript (Egerton MS 1994, British Library), first printed in 1849. Standard edition: The Plays and Poems of Philip Massinger (Oxford University Press, 1976).

title: The Maid of Honour
description: Massinger's tragicomedy of Camiola, the 'maid of honour' of Siena, who refuses to ransom the captured noble Bertoldo until he pledges himself to her, and who finally retires to a convent rather than marry a prince's brother.
plot_or_argument: Bertoldo, captured by the King of Tunis, is ransomed by Camiola; he repays her with ingratitude; she brings him to justice, and, her honour vindicated, she takes the veil.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a double plot of court intrigue and moral constancy.
principal_characters: Camiola; Bertoldo; Roberto; Ferdinand; Fulgoso; Adorni; Clarinda
historical_context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men at the Red Bull c. 1622 and published in 1632.
literary_significance: An early and influential Massinger tragicomedy, notable for its strong, morally autonomous heroine; it was adapted by Johnson in 1730 as The Successful Pyrate.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1632. Standard edition: The Plays and Poems of Philip Massinger (Oxford University Press, 1976).

title: The Unnatural Combat
description: Massinger's dark tragedy in which the Marseilles admiral Malefort, under pressure from his son, kills him in single combat, and the son's ghost returns to expose the father's crimes.
plot_or_argument: The young Malefort, corrupted by the villain Beauford junior, demands a combat with his father; the father kills him; the ghost reveals the unnatural deed and the father's earlier crime, and Malefort dies in madness.
narrative_structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a ghost and a catastrophic recognition.
principal_characters: Malefort senior; Malefort junior; Beauford; Theocrine; Montrevile; Rochefort
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men at the Globe c. 1624-26 and published in 1639.
literary_significance: One of Massinger's most powerful tragedies, notable for its psychological intensity and its treatment of paternal guilt; it was long thought to have influenced later Jacobean and Caroline revenge drama.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1639. Standard edition: The Plays and Poems of Philip Massinger (Oxford University Press, 1976).

title: The Staple of News
description: Ben Jonson's late satirical comedy on the new business of news-gathering, in which a 'Staple of News' is established to supply the gulls of London with fabricated intelligence and young Pecunia is courted by fortune hunters.
plot_or_argument: Thomas Barber opens an office that manufactures news for the town; the young heir Pennyboy junior squanders his fortune chasing novelty; the Censure and Prologue figures comment throughout, and the play ends with the Staple's collapse.
narrative_structure: Five acts with intermeans in which a Censure and a Prologue debate the play's own merits.
principal_characters: Thomas Barber; Pennyboy junior; Pennyboy senior; Pecunia junior; the Censure; the Prologue; the Register; Fitton
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in February 1626 and published in the first folio of Jonson's works in 1631; it attacks the newly emerging news-sheet industry.
literary_significance: Jonson's most explicit commentary on the new print culture and journalism, and an important document in the history of the news; it was long considered one of his weaker late plays.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Workes of Beniamin Jonson (1631), the second folio. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of Ben Jonson (G. A. Wilkes, ed., Oxford University Press, 1981-2).

title: The Magnetic Lady; or, Humours Reconciled
description: Jonson's last comedy, in which the learned Lady Loadstone acts as a magnet drawing a set of humours characters together and reconciling them through a marriage plot and a discovered heiress.
plot_or_argument: Lady Loadstone's household gathers a soldier, a parson, a courtier, a physician, and others; a concealed heiress, Pleasance, is discovered, the suitors are tested, and the humours are reconciled in marriage.
narrative_structure: Five acts with an unusual induction in which two audience figures discuss the play.
principal_characters: Lady Loadstone; Pleasance; Compass; Bias; Parson Palate; Captain Ironside; Sir Moth Interest; Doctor Rut
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in 1632 and published in the 1640 folio.
literary_significance: Jonson's farewell to comedy and a final attempt to reconcile the humours tradition with a romantic plot; its induction is a rare piece of Jonsonian meta-theatrical commentary.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Workes of Benjamin Jonson, second folio (1640-1). Standard edition: The Complete Plays of Ben Jonson (G. A. Wilkes, ed., OUP, 1981-2).
